title: Record European Heatwave Forces Uniqlo Store Closures
snippet: A record European heatwave forced Uniqlo parent Fast Retailing to temporarily close some stores, as extreme heat kept shoppers away despite expectations of
extractedText: Record European Heatwave Forces Uniqlo Store ClosuresInternational|Published 2026.07.12. 15:10:52|By Lim Hye-rin|Summary|SaveAAAPedestrians pass by a Uniqlo store. Photo for illustrative purposes. News1A record-breaking heatwave sweeping across Europe has disrupted operations at global SPA brand Uniqlo. Summer heat typically boosts sales of functional clothing and short-sleeved products, but this time it hurt sales as consumers avoided going outside altogether. Industry analysts say climate change is emerging as a new management variable for the retail sector.According to Britain's Financial Times (FT) on the 11th, Uniqlo's parent company Fast Retailing temporarily suspended operations or shortened business hours at some European stores last month. The company had expected expanded sales of summer products such as linen shirts and functional clothing, but shoppers stayed away amid the record heat, and the anticipated sales effect failed to materialize.Takeshi Okazaki, Fast Retailing's chief financial officer (CFO), said at the quarterly earnings announcement, "Cooling systems in European cities were not designed to account for this level of heat, so an extremely dangerous situation temporarily arose." He added, "There were stores that could not operate during this period." He explained that all European stores are now operating normally after some closures.Fast Retailing plans to review its store operation systems and supply chain response framework in the wake of the heatwave. The company intends to inspect cooling facilities at European stores while continuing to develop functional clothing that can be worn comfortably even in extreme heat.The case is seen as shaking the existing formula that summer heat necessarily leads to increased clothing sales. Generally, when temperatures rise, demand for short-sleeved and functional clothing increases, but extreme heat beyond a certain level can dampen consumers' outdoor activity itself, reducing visits to offline stores.A Greggs store in London, England. Reuters/Yonhap NewsThe heatwave damage was not limited to Uniqlo. British bakery chain Greggs closed 11 stores in the UK for two days, and British retailer Marks & Spencer (M&S) is preparing response plans assuming a maximum temperature of 45 degrees Celsius in case of refrigeration system failures at some stores. H&M is also reviewing adjustments to its clothing lineup in consideration of climate change bringing longer stretches of hot weather.European companies are also moving faster to respond to the heat, such as moving up working hours or expanding cooling facilities. Eurostar, the European high-speed rail operator, plans to design new trains to be introduced in the future to operate in environments of up to 55 degrees Celsius, higher than the existing 45 degrees. The measure reflects the possibility of increased strain on tracks and power facilities from recurring heatwaves.However, there are also forecasts that the heatwave could become an opportunity for Uniqlo in the long term. Analysts say demand for breathable and functional clothing developed for Japan's hot summers could expand in Europe as well.Indeed, Fast Retailing's quarterly net profit through the end of May this year rose 39.1 percent from a year earlier to 146.7 billion yen (about 1.364 trillion won). The gain was driven by continued new store openings in Europe and the United States and growth in overseas businesses. The company raised its annual operating profit forecast for fiscal year 2026 to 730 billion yen from the previous 700 billion yen.However, the situation was different in the Japanese market. Cooler-than-expected weather in June reduced clothing demand, and combined with the impact of price increases due to the weak yen, sales in Japan fell 14 percent from the same period last year. The FT analyzed that while Europe, along with the United States, is cited as Uniqlo's fastest-growing market, recurring heatwaves could act as a new variable that changes companies' investment and cost structures going forward.#Uniqlo#FastRetailing#Heatwave#ClimateChange#RetailNews#Europe#SPABrandOriginal reporting by Lim Hye-rin for Seoul Economic Daily.AI-translated from Korean.
